title: Design, with a capital D
principle: Design is not decoration applied after engineering — it is how the thing works. Start from what the person is trying to do and work backwards to the simplest interaction that does it.

anchor.title: “Design is how it works” — the Jobs formulation the estate's Designer role is built on
anchor.author: Steve Jobs
anchor.note: **Anchor unconfirmed.** The formulation is from the 2003 *New York Times Magazine* profile linked above; the candidates for what actually did the shaping are that piece, the MP3-to-CD whiteboard story, a keynote, or a specific product. Asked as [Q2b](../../admin/comms.html#q2b).

quote.text: Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.
quote.note: Quoted to be examined, and it is the whole entry in one line: design is named as a property of the mechanism rather than of the surface.

rows.pattern: Design is how it works, not how it looks
rows.where: The estate's Designer role definition, which is built on the formulation and extends it to coherence between internal structure and external experience

rows.pattern: Start from the user's intent and work backwards (the Ive principle)
rows.where: The NotebookLM case-study brief, in a section named for the principle, with the MP3-to-CD story as the worked example

rows.pattern: Good design is invisible — you notice it by reverting and feeling the loss
rows.where: **The Jonathan Ive test**: *is it simpler? would reverting feel worse?* — a mandatory validator for every UI change

rows.pattern: Simplicity as subtraction — the feature removed rather than the feature added
rows.where: Implied by the Ive test's first half and not separately enforced. Nothing records what was taken out of a change
rows.source: the same brief; the test states the criterion, nothing records the outcome

rows.pattern: The same discipline applied to non-visual surfaces — an API, a CLI, a file format
rows.where: Nowhere. The validator is scoped to UI changes, and the estate's public surface is mostly not UI
